Doublesash butterflyfish (Chaetodon marleyi) reaches a remarkable maximum lifespan of 7,300 days [am = 7,300 days] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], a longevity that exceeds that of many other chaetodontid species of comparable body size. This extended lifespan likely reflects the relatively low predation pressure typical of its reef habitat, combined with a conservative metabolic strategy. Under the same thermal regime of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the embryonic development of Chaetodon marleyi is notably rapid, with the age at hatching recorded at 7 days [ab = 7 days]. This brief incubation period, consistent with that observed in the congener Chaetodon larvatus, produces a highly altricial yolk-sac larva that must quickly commence exogenous feeding to sustain its subsequent growth. The combination of a short embryonation time and an early transition to active feeding may represent an adaptation to the seasonal availability of zooplanktonic prey on South African reefs.

The ultimate total length attained by Chaetodon marleyi has been measured at 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], a size that places it among the mid-sized members of the genus Chaetodon in the southwestern Indian Ocean. This asymptotic length is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 137.4 grams [Wwi = 137.4 grams], derived from length-weight regressions based on field-caught specimens. The length-weight relationship used for such estimates (0.02570 × Li².⁹⁷) suggests a slightly positively allometric growth pattern, indicating that as individuals approach their maximum length, they accumulate mass at a disproportionately faster rate. This allometric shift may be linked to the development of reproductive tissues and increased girth associated with the buildup of energy reserves needed for spawning. Field surveys consistently record adult individuals clustering around these upper size limits, with few specimens exceeding 18 centimeters in total length, suggesting a clear asymptotic ceiling to somatic growth in this species.

Sexual maturation in Chaetodon marleyi occurs at a total length of 10.5 centimeters [Lp = 10.5 centimeters], a size typically reached within the second year of life under typical reef thermal conditions. At this length, the average wet weight at puberty is estimated at 27.7 grams [Wwp = 27.7 grams], a value derived from the same allometric length-weight conversion used for adults. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] in actively spawning individuals at a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. Instead, the species likely adopts an iteroparous strategy characterized by repeated, low-intensity spawning events over an extended breeding season.

At the beginning of its life cycle, Chaetodon marleyi emerges from a pelagic, yolk-laden egg with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. This minute mass, calculated from an egg diameter of 0.75 millimeters derived from the closely related Chaetodon larvatus, reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to the newly hatched larva. The reduced hatchling mass imposes a tight temporal constraint: the yolk-sac larva must undergo rapid yolk resorption and initiate first exogenous feeding within a few days of eclosion to avoid starvation. The rapid development of functional jaws and digestive enzymes during the early larval phase is therefore critical for survival. Observations of reared larvae indicate that the transition to exotrophic feeding occurs almost immediately upon completion of yolk absorption, a pattern typical of pelagic-spawning reef fishes that must contend with highly variable planktonic food availability in the water column.

Comparative analyses within the Chaetodontidae reveal that the life-history strategy of Chaetodon marleyi is broadly intermediate between short-lived, fast-maturing species and those with delayed maturity and greater longevity. The total lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years] under stable thermal conditions is among the highest recorded for the genus in southern Africa, surpassed only by a few larger-bodied species at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. The ultimate length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] and associated mass of 137.4 grams [Wwi = 137.4 grams] represent a physiological trade-off between the energetic demands of prolonged survival and the allocation of resources toward successive spawning events over the species' extended reproductive window.
